sections.title: Level 3 Strategy
sections.content: At Level 3, the subject is often hidden or the sentence structure is inverted. Step 1: Read the entire sentence carefully and identify the main clause. Step 2: Find the real subject, even if it appears after the verb. Step 3: Identify whether the subject is singular or plural. Step 4: Apply relative pronoun rules or special noun rules if needed. Step 5: Temporarily remove middle phrases and check the correct agreement between the subject and the verb.

sections.title: Relative Pronouns (Who, Which, That)
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the relative pronoun (who, which, that). Step 2: Find its antecedent, the noun it refers to. Step 3: Determine whether the antecedent is singular or plural. Step 4: Use the verb according to that antecedent. Step 5: Recheck the sentence structure. Example: 'He is one of the men who have completed the task.' Here 'who' refers to 'men', so 'have' is correct.

sections.title: Inverted Sentences
sections.content: Step 1: Check whether the sentence begins with 'here', 'there', or a prepositional phrase. Step 2: Identify that the real subject appears after the verb. Step 3: Determine whether the subject is singular or plural. Step 4: Choose the verb accordingly. Step 5: Mentally convert the sentence to normal order to confirm. Example: 'Among the trees stands a beautiful house.' Here the subject 'house' is singular.

sections.title: Deceptive Nouns
sections.content: Step 1: Identify nouns that may look plural or singular but behave differently. Step 2: Understand their actual meaning. Step 3: If the noun is singular in meaning, use a singular verb. Step 4: If the noun is plural in meaning, use a plural verb. Step 5: Remember common examples. Example: 'Mathematics is interesting.' But 'The police are investigating the case.'

sections.title: Subject-Verb with Long Phrases
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the subject. Step 2: Temporarily remove the prepositional or participial phrases between the subject and the verb. Step 3: Determine the number of the subject. Step 4: Use the verb accordingly. Step 5: Read the full sentence again to confirm correctness. Example: 'The quality of the apples in that basket is good.'

sections.title: 'Many a / Many an' Rule
sections.content: Step 1: Check whether the sentence contains 'many a' or 'many an'. Step 2: The noun following it is singular. Step 3: The verb must also be singular. Step 4: Even though the meaning suggests plurality, grammatically it remains singular. Step 5: Confirm the sentence structure. Example: 'Many a student has solved the problem.'

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Level 3 questions, the subject is often hidden or misleading. With relative pronouns, identifying the antecedent is essential. In inverted sentences, the subject appears after the verb. Deceptive nouns require understanding their true meaning. Long phrases should be temporarily removed to check agreement. After 'many a', the verb is always singular.

tricks.title: Relative Pronoun Trick
tricks.explanation: After who/which/that, the verb agrees with the antecedent.
tricks.example: He is one of the players who have scored centuries.

tricks.title: Inversion Quick Check
tricks.explanation: If a sentence starts with here, there, or a prepositional phrase, find the real subject after the verb.
tricks.example: There are many books on the table.

tricks.title: Singular-Looking Nouns
tricks.explanation: Words like mathematics, news, measles appear plural but take a singular verb.

tricks.title: Plural Meaning Nouns
tricks.explanation: Nouns like police, cattle, clergy always take plural verbs.
tricks.example: The police are searching for the thief.

tricks.title: Remove the Phrase Trick
tricks.explanation: Remove phrases between the subject and the verb to identify correct agreement.
tricks.example: The list of items is long.

tricks.title: 'Many a' Rule
tricks.explanation: 'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb.
tricks.example: Many a player has tried to break the record.

tricks.title: Check the True Subject
tricks.explanation: Do not get confused by the noun near the verb; find the real subject.
tricks.example: The bouquet of flowers smells sweet.

tricks.title: Reverse the Sentence Trick
tricks.explanation: Mentally convert inverted sentences into normal order to identify the subject.
tricks.example: A beautiful temple stands on the hill.
